newsitem.title: UK: Sterling powers ahead to new 52-month high vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Sterling powers ahead to new 52-month high vs mark.

text.p: Sterling powered ahead on Tuesday, jumping some two pfennigs against the mark, and setting fresh 52-month highs above 2.73 against the German currency.
Sterling's ride against the mark on Tuesday was attributed more to mark weakness than sterling strength.
"Now that the G-7 meeting is over, the market is focused on the mark," said a trader at a Swiss bank.

Traders attributed overriding mark weakness to a column in The Times newspaper on Tuesday talking of German economic woes and some even said a BBC report on Monday saying rising unemployment would push Germany's 1997 budget deficit to 3.5 percent of GDP was a factor.

In response to the BBC report, Germany's finance ministry said there was "no reason" to revise its forecast for a budget deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product. The Maastricht limit for single currency membership is a GDP/budget deficit ratio of 3.0 percent. "It's all mark weakness, the market is still factoring in Germany's huge jump in unemployment figures," said a senior dealer at a German bank.

Germany's January unemployment leapt by half a million to a post-war record 4.66 million, underlining Germany's economic problems that some dare to say jeopardise its entry into the single currency from the start.
The finance ministry spokesman said the figures had not altered Bonn's EMU expectations.
At 1223 GMT sterling was trading at 2.7370/80, just off fresh 52-month highs of 2.7400 marks hit earlier, up from 2.7130/40 marks in late Europe on Monday.
Against the dollar, sterling was steady, trading at $1.6390/00 against $1.6380/90 in late dealings on Monday.
Aside from German weakness, sterling is also benefiting from its status as a "safe haven", unlikely to join EMU at the outset.
"It is continuing the trend, with sterling gaining from the "safe haven" argument," said one economist.
Currency analysts said mark weakness against the dollar was also buoying up sterling against the mark.
The market is now awaiting the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report and January unemployment figures on Wednesday.
The Bank of England is expected to renew its warnings about a pickup in inflation in the next two years and strongly urge a tightening in monetary policy.
The report, due for release at 1130 GMT on Wednesday, will be one of the last high-profile platforms for the central bank to air its views on monetary policy before the election.
"What is becoming clearer is that there won't be any rate rises before the election," said Francis Breedon, senior foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.

Breedon said soft producer price figures, which set fresh lows in January, would indicate that British inflation is benign. Data on Monday showed output prices rose just 1.5 percent year-on-year in January, the lowest rate of increase since October 1986. Core output prices, excluding food, drink, tobacco and petroleum, rose 0.6 percent on a year earlier - the lowest rate in 30 years.
